title: SafetyNet QBR: runway, cost acceleration & on-call alignment
summary: Quarterly health review focused on usage trends, cost acceleration during recent campaign, latency outliers in US-West, and roadmap alignment for a private deployment pilot. Agreed to run a targeted benchmark on canary traffic, share security artifacts, and propose a 3-month reserved capacity plan. Action items and next steps captured.
action_items: Maya Chen - send updated reserved capacity pricing sheet and example commitment tiers - due: 2027-06-18
Omar Patel - run 1-hour canary benchmark (50 RPS, 512 tokens avg) with KV cache scenarios and share raw traces - due: 2027-06-21
Elena Ruiz - schedule follow-up 30m ops workshop with customer's platform and oncall teams - due: 2027-06-20
Jordan Lee - provide example production prompt set and three representative user journeys for fidelity checks - due: 2027-06-22
Luis Fernandez - confirm required compliance docs and KMS/HSM constraints; share any enclave/HSM serials - due: 2027-06-19
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing and pilot CD with baseline SLOs
Run canary benchmark and review tail-latency traces together
Ops workshop for on-call runbook and escalation integration
Security team to exchange SOC2 scope and KMS integration notes
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-15 16:30 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Omar Patel, Elena Ruiz (Redwood) / Jordan Lee, Priya Kapoor, Luis Fernandez, Aisha Khan, Samir Bose (SafetyNet)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll start quick. this is our quarterly health check with SafetyNet, want to go over the spike last month, cost movement, and next steps for the dedicated pilot you asked about. Omar and Elena are here to cover the deep tech and ops bits.

[00:18] Jordan Lee: thanks Maya, yeah appreciate it. We had a big conversion push last week and usage jumped, costs spiked higher than expected. main ask: how do we avoid making that permanent and what would a dedicated/reserved plan look like?

[00:32] Aisha Khan: to add, finance is concerned about token burn during peak windows, we need predictability. also want to understand if we can throttle or autoscale without losing SLO.

[00:45] Omar Patel: yeah, quick note: from the traces you shared there were some long tail outliers in US-West at 95th/99th, looks like KV cache misses during heavy prefix variance, plus a small fraction of requests that hit larger max tokens. we can tune batching and prefix caching to lower p99.

[01:05] Priya Kapoor: is that a software-level change or do we need different hardware? our platform is on GCP us-west2 primarily.

[01:12] Omar Patel: mostly config: batching windows, active KV cache usage, and model variant routing — e.g., route best-effort traffic to quantized variants when under pressure. if you want absolute lowest latency under sustained high throughput then dedicated GPUs help with predictability.

[01:30] Samir Bose: can you explain the tradeoff again — quantized models reduce cost but affect quality? how big is the difference for our prompt set?

[01:38] Omar Patel: generally quantization (4-bit or int8) lowers memory and token compute which reduces per-token cost; fidelity regression is workload dependent. for many retrieval-augmented generation prompts the difference is negligible, but we'll validate with your representative journey. Jordan, if you share 20 sample flows we can benchmark.

[01:56] Jordan Lee: yep will do.

[02:02] Elena Ruiz: on the operations side, we noticed your on-call got paged for degraded responses during the spike. we suggested an on-call integration runbook that ties Redwood route fallback to a low-cost model and sends enriched traces to your observability stack. this avoids noisy alerts while keeping users served.

[02:22] Luis Fernandez: security question — for a private deployment we need KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and confirmation of encryption in transit + at rest. Also what is Redwood's SOC2 scope?

[02:34] Maya Chen: good call. we'll share SOC2 docs and our SOC2-in-scope boundary. we support customer-managed KMS for private deployments and can integrate with common HSM providers; Omar will include specifics in the follow-up.

[02:48] Luis Fernandez: and SSO? we use SAML with Okta.

[02:52] Elena Ruiz: SAML/SSO is supported for console access and RBAC. we can demo SAML mapping in the ops workshop.

[03:05] Aisha Khan: finance wants scenarios: if we commit to 3 months reserved capacity what savings do we get vs pay-as-you-go, and what's the elasticity for spikes?

[03:15] Maya Chen: we'll propose a tiered reserved plan: baseline capacity for the 95th percentile, a burst pool for temporary spikes, and overflow to hosted at slightly higher cost if dedicated pool is saturated. I'll include math examples for your last three months of usage.

[03:38] Jordan Lee: curious — for the overflow, are there hard fails? we can't have user-facing failures during peak campaign windows.

[03:45] Omar Patel: no hard fails — you can configure automatic fallback policies: route to a smaller model variant, region fallback, or queued responses. for mission-critical user flows we recommend pinned instances + synchronous canary checks.

[04:05] Priya Kapoor: can we get a run of a canary profile? something that simulates your campaign traffic pattern.

[04:10] Maya Chen: absolutely, Omar can run a 1-hour canary at 50 RPS with KV cache on/off and we can analyze tail latency, error rates, and cost per 1k tokens.

[04:22] Omar Patel: yep I'll include CPU/GPU utilization, model load times, and traces for any >500ms tails. also will test quantized variant to show cost delta.

[04:40] Samir Bose: what about rollout controls — can we do canary then A/B then full? we want to avoid full-surface regressions.

[04:47] Elena Ruiz: Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback. we'll recommend a rollout policy: 10% canary for 2 hours, validate eval prompts, then 50% for 24h, then 100% with autoscaling rules.

[05:05] Jordan Lee: eval prompts — can Redwood run automatic quality regressions? we need to ensure no drop in key metrics (precision on extraction tasks).

[05:12] Omar Patel: yes, our Optimize tooling runs quality guards against a curated prompt set; it can raise alerts on regression thresholds and block rollouts. we'll onboard your prompt set into that eval harness.

[05:28] Luis Fernandez: timeline questions — how long to get Private deployed in our VPC if we sign a pilot?

[05:35] Maya Chen: typical private pilot across VPC with customer-managed KMS is 4-6 weeks: initial infra template, networking and firewall, SSO config, and a small capacity roll. if on-prem air-gapped it's longer.

[05:49] Aisha Khan: ok that fits some internal timelines. we have an exec review in two weeks, could you get pricing and a short SLO proposal before then?

[05:57] Maya Chen: yes—we'll send pricing and a 3-month SLO proposal by Friday.

[06:03] Elena Ruiz: ops note: during the spike your alerting thresholds were narrow; we recommend synthetic canaries for critical flows, and to forward enriched traces with token-level latencies to your APM to reduce noisy on-call pages.

[06:20] Priya Kapoor: technical nit — does Redwood expose KV cache hit rates per route? we want to instrument cache effectiveness.

[06:26] Omar Patel: yes, we expose per-route metrics: KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, queue wait time, and per-token CPU/GPU utilization. we'll add those to the dashboard we share.

[06:40] Samir Bose: competitors — we evaluated Anthropic and also tried to run our own model farm. Anthropic had better single-request latency but the integration and cost profile made it trickier; running a self-hosted farm had ops overhead. Redwood's selling point was unified tooling and predictable SLOs.

[06:58] Maya Chen: thanks — that context helps. ok last section: recap and decisions. agreed items: Redwood to run canary benchmark (Omar), Redwood to send pricing and reserved plan (Maya), ops workshop (Elena), SafetyNet to share prompt set and compliance constraints (Jordan, Luis).

[07:20] Jordan Lee: quick clarifying question — for the reserved plan, will we be able to pause baseline for a week without penalties? during slow times we can't justify burn.

[07:30] Maya Chen: we can include a pause policy in the proposal; typically reserved commitments allow limited pause windows per quarter with prorated billing — we'll show exact terms.

[07:42] Luis Fernandez: and for KMS, can you confirm bring-your-own-key (BYOK) flow? we need to keep control of key lifecycle.

[07:48] Omar Patel: BYOK is supported for Private; Redwood never stores plaintext key material. we can outline the HSM integrations and key rotation policy in the security packet.

[07:59] Aisha Khan: thanks, that's helpful. finance will review pricing and want to see expected monthly burn for the last three months with proposed reserved discount.

[08:10] Maya Chen: noted. we'll attach a worked example. Elena, can you send the ops workshop invite for next week?

[08:16] Elena Ruiz: will do.

[08:20] Maya Chen: ok great, appreciate everyone's time. short recap on next steps and action items in the calendar note. we can reconvene after the canary benchmark to review traces and finalize pilot commit.

[08:35] Jordan Lee: thanks all.

[08:40] (meeting ends)

Notes on audio/transcript: occasional overlaps, the automated transcript had a few mis-hearings around acronyms (HSM sounded like 'HSM' sometimes 'H S M' or 'ash em'), and 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash' in a few places. timestamps in the body are approximations every ~30-90s.
